title: Not tight-fisted, not wasteful
hook: don't chain your hand to your neck nor stretch it all the way out (17:29)
tomorrow: Don't follow what you don't know

segments.voice: Yesterday, birr al-walidayn, goodness to parents, and your line was not even a sigh. Did someone older ask you something again? How did you answer? Day four hundred fifty-nine.

Hold your hand up in front of you. Now pull it in tight and press your fist to your throat, as if it were tied there. That's one picture. Now fling it out, fingers wide open, as far as your arm will reach, so anything you were holding falls through. That's the other. Surah seventeen uses both pictures, in one verse, to talk about money. Neither is the way. Today: what's in between.

The verses just before set the scene. Give the relative his due, and the needy, and the traveler, and don't squander, tabdhir, a word that comes from scattering seed carelessly. Then 17:29, in Pickthall's translation: "And let not thy hand be chained to thy neck nor open it with a complete opening, lest thou sit down rebuked, denuded." The chained hand is the miser: it can't reach out to anyone. The hand opened all the way is the opposite trouble: everything spills, and you end up sitting down with nothing, blamed and stripped bare. Notice the verse doesn't praise either extreme. It doesn't say the person who gives everything away is the hero. Another surah, Al-Furqan, describes the servants of the Merciful as people who, when they spend, are neither wasteful nor stingy, but take a stand between the two. There's a scene in Bukhari that shows how the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ applied this. His companion Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas fell badly ill and wanted to give away all his wealth in charity. The Prophet said no. Half? No. A third? A third, the Prophet said, and a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than to leave them dependent on others. So generosity has a shape. It reaches out, and it also keeps enough to carry the people who depend on you. This week we're walking through the commands of Al-Isra: no sigh at your parents yesterday, and today, a hand neither tied nor emptied. The middle hand.
screen: `TABDHIR: SEED SCATTERED CARELESSLY.` · `THE CHAINED HAND, THE SPILLING HAND.` · `SA'D: NOT ALL, NOT HALF. A THIRD.` · `GENEROSITY HAS A SHAPE.` · then, large: `THE MIDDLE HAND.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open in your lap, palms up, relaxed, not clenched and not stretched. Feel what that middle position is like. Then think about your spending lately. Is there one place your hand has been tied, where you held back from someone who needed it? Is there one place it's been flung open, money going out with no thought? Don't judge it. Just notice which side you lean toward. Then choose one small, sensible adjustment for today. The bell holds the time.
Not tight-fisted, and not wasteful either: a hand neither chained to the neck nor flung all the way open. Today's word.
Your line: the middle hand. Today, spend moderately: before one purchase, ask whether it's the chained hand, the spilling hand, or the middle one. Day four hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim teaching on money draws on 17:26–29 and 25:67 to call for moderation between stinginess and waste; Islamic law limits bequests to charity to a third of an estate, following the hadith of Sa'd.

it warns against the hand opened all the way, as well as the chained one.
Al-Furqan describes a stand between waste and stinginess

fork.setup: you're Sa'd, very ill, and you want to give your whole fortune to charity. you ask the Prophet. what does he say?
options: all of it: charity is always best.
a third, and a third is a lot; leave your heirs well off.
none: keep it all for your family.
fork.reveal: a third. better to leave your heirs well off than dependent on others (Bukhari). generosity, with a shape.

original.note: Arabic: chained to your neck (17:29), the picture of the tight fist.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't spend too much.
what it means: don't be stingy and don't be reckless; give, and keep enough to carry those who depend on you.
what a scholar hears: tabdhir comes from badhr, scattering seed; the hadith of Sa'd is the basis for the one-third limit on bequests in Islamic law.
